latin.2689: XIX. Quin illud ipsum obsequium quod fideles legi exhibent suis defectibus & naevis non caret, & in illis ipsis operibus quae conformiter legi edunt summam ἀκρίβειαν, legis non assequuntur; semperque illo respectu restat iis materia profectus, & aliquid ad quod contendere debeant. Quod evidens est Pauli Apost. exemplo. Neque enim facile reperietur aliquis cui tantam gratiae mensuram indulserit Christus. Et tamen ipse fatetur se nondum esse perfectum, & se ad ulteriora perpetuo contendere. Phil. 3. Non inquit, quod jam apprehenderim, aut jam perfectus sim: sequor autem, si quo modo comprehendam, in quo & comprehensus sum a Christo Jesu. Fratres, ego me non arbitror comprehendisse. Unum autem ago, quae quidem retro sunt obliviscens, ad ea vero quae sunt priora me extendens, ad destinatum persequor, ad bravium supernae vocationis Dei in Christo Jesu.
latin.2690: XX. At, inquies, Apostolus ipse eo in loco supponit quosdam esse perfectos, & se in eorum numero collocat. Verbis enim citatis subjungit, quicunque ergo perfecti sumus hoc sentiamus. Et 1 Cor. 2. Sapientiam, inquit, loquimur inter perfectos. Multisque viris sanctis in scriptura testimonium perhibetur quod perfecti fuerint. Ita de Noe dicitur Gen. 6. Noe vir justus fuit atque perfectus in generationibus suis, & ambulavit cum Deo. Et de Job Deus ipse Satanam alloquens dicit, Nunquid considerasti servum meum Job, quod non sit ei similis in terra, Isch Tham, i. Vir integer, sive, perfectus, & rectus, ac timens Deum, & recedens a malo? cap. 1. & 2. Imo David, Psal. 18. non veretur sibi talem perfectionem tribuere. Fui, inquit, immaculatus, sive perfectus, cum eo, & custodivi me ab iniquitate mea. Et retribuit mihi Dominus secundum justitiam meam, & secundum puritatem manuum mearum in conspectu oculorum ejus.
latin.2691: XXI. Quae difficultas ut solvatur observanda est duplex perfectionis distinctio. Est enim perfectio quaedam absolute sic dicta, alia vero secundum quid & comparate tantum. Absolute perfectum est illud cui in suo genere nihil deest. Comparate vero perfecta dicuntur ea quae licet a summa perfectione absint, multa tamen superant alia ejusdem generis, cum quibus instituitur eorum comparatio. Quum dicimus in hac vita nullos esse perfectos, sive qui perfectum divinae voluntati obsequium praebeant, istud intelligimus de perfectione absoluta, quae pervenit ad summum, & ad quam nihil addi potest, quo sensu Paulus agnoscit se nondum esse perfectum, quia nondum pervenerat ad illum gradum amoris & obsequii erga Deum, ad quem evecti sunt beati spiritus cum Christo regnantes; quorum non tantum cognitio, sed obsequium etiam & amor, nullum amplius potest sumere incrementum, cum totis omnino viribus, totoque voluntatis affectu ferantur in Deum. Verum hoc non obstat quo minus fideles qui virtute caeteris praecellunt, & qui in veritatis divinae notitia, & pietatis ac justitiae studio majores progressus fecerunt, perfecti nominentur, non quidem simpliciter, sed respectu eorum qui multum illis hac in parte cedunt, quique sunt adhuc, ut Paulus loquitur, infantes in Christo, & quodammodo carnales, prae illis qui singulari ratione spirituales appellantur, ut videre est 1 Cor. 3. Et hi sunt inter Christianos, ut sic dicam, adultiores, & aetatis ac staturae, si ita loqui licet, magis provectae, quos Paulus locis ante citatis perfectos vocat, dum ait, Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, &, Quicunque perfecti sumus hoc sentiamus.
latin.2692: XXII. Huic distinctioni affinis est altera, juxta quam distingui solet perfectio in perfectionem partium & perfectionem graduum. Perfecta secundum gradus obedientia illa est quae attingit summum perfectionis gradum, & per quam aliquis legi ita perfecte se conformat & subjicit, ut in eo nihil prorsus desiderari queat, neque hoc respectu possit in melius proficere. Hac ratione contendimus, & per se manifestum est legem a nullo perfecte in hac vita impleri. Verum obedientia quae multum a summo gradu perfectionis abest, nihilominus esse & dici potest perfecta secundum partes; quoniam respectu partium, sive essentialium, sive integrantium, nihil illi deest eorum quae necessaria sunt ut sit obedientia vera & Deo accepta. Hoc sensu perfecta est obedientia piorum in hac vita, & hoc respectu fideles qui sunt per Christi gratiam renovati, & spiritu illius ducuntur, perfecte Dei legem implere possunt, id est, verum & sincerum, Deoque gratum obsequium mandatis illius praebere. Nec enim essentialis ejusmodi perfectio aliud est quam ipsius rei veritas atque sinceritas.
latin.2693: XXIII. Ut autem istud clarius innotescat, observandum est ad hoc, ut obedientia nostra vera & sincera sit, tria praecipue requiri. Primum est ut praestetur non tantum corpore & opere externo, sed interno quoque animi affectu. Neque enim quicquam prodest ea facere quae lex jubet, nisi id fiat ex Dei amore, & voluntatis illius implendae ac gloriae ejus promovendae studio. Ut nec satis est quendam affectum Deo obsequendi habere, nisi mandata ejus, quum res id postulat, ipso opere compleantur. Praeterea non sufficit ad veram obedientiam ut quaedam Dei mandata, reliquis neglectis, servemus: sed necesse est ut omnibus legis Divinae praeceptis nos serio subjiciamus, illaque, cum sese offert occasio, implere studeamus. Denique debet esse obedientia nostra constans & perseverans: Nec satis est Deo ad tempus obsequi, sed in ejus obsequio, tam per res adversas quam per res secundas, ad finem usque perseverandum est.
latin.2694: XXIV. Horum omnium respectu nihil deest obedientiae eorum qui vere pii & per spiritum Dei regeniti sunt. Nec enim corpore tantum Deo serviunt, sed mentem & affectus voluntati ejus subjiciunt. Nec solum opere praestant quae lege praecipiuntur; sed etiam in eo gloriam Dei spectant, & amore illius moventur. Non his, aut illis mandatis duntaxat obedire satagunt; sed universae legi Dei & singulis ejus mandatis sese conformare nituntur. Nec solum ad aliquod tempus, & quandiu res prospere fluunt, sed etiam quum ingruunt tentationes & persecutiones, & ad ultimum usque vitae spiritum mandata Dei ob oculos habent, & actiones suas ad eorum normam exigunt.
latin.2695: XXV. Itaque jure merito potest eorum obedientiae tribui perfectio illa, quae perfectio Partium in Scholis appellari solet. Siquidem integrae legi, & universis illius praeceptis, tum corporis actus, tum animi affectus, idque constanter & perseveranter exigere conantur. Et certe, nisi hoc esset, scriptura fidelibus non tribueret justitiam & sanctitatem veram, dum ait, illos indui novo homine, qui creatur secundum Deum, in justitia & sanctitate veritatis, Ephes. 4. Nam vera justitia non est, quae respectu partium, ad essentiam justitiae omnino pertinentium, manca & mutila est. Et haec est illa perfectio cujus nomine laudantur Job & Noe, & quam David sibi ipsi tribuere non formidat. Etenim per perfectionem solum ibi designatur integritas atque sinceritas sanctorum istorum virorum. Siquidem vox Hebraea Tham sive thamim, quam ibi Interpretes per perfectum exponunt, integrum & sincerum proprie significat.
latin.2696: XXVI. Negamus igitur fideles perfecte Dei legem implere posse, si sermo sit, de perfectione quae absoluta dicitur & graduum: tum quia omnes illi, non minus quam caeteri homines, per naturam sunt peccatores; tum quia post acceptam gratiam non desinunt in multis offendere, & gravibus etiam lapsibus obnoxii manent: neque in bonis ipsis operibus quae faciunt summam illam ἀκρίβειαν, quam lex in rigore suo exigit, assequuntur. Et tamen cum scriptura dicimus & docemus, fideles Dei mandata per Christi gratiam servare, & aliquo etiam modo legem implere, quoniam veram Deoque probatam obedientiam legi divinae, secundum omnia illius praecepta, exhibent: quae obedientia licet multum infra summam perfectionem subsidat, nihilominus, juxta scripturae stylum, perfecta dici potest; quoniam vera atque sincera est, nec quicquam ei deest eorum quae ad obedientiae verae & Deo acceptae, naturam & integritatem necessario requiruntur.
latin.2697: XXVII. Atque haec Sententiae Orthodoxae explicatio diligenter observanda est propter doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, qui in hac quaestione, ut in multis aliis, Scholae Reformatae doctrinam, aut non intelligunt, aut studio pervertunt. Siquidem Theologis Protestantibus tribuunt quod simpliciter negent Christi fideles Dei mandata servare posse, & legem ita implere, ut quaedam eorum opera justa appellari possint. Imo quod doceant legem plane impossibilem esse homini etiam per Christi gratiam justificato: adeo ut non possit ulla bona opera facere, nec in eo sit ulla vera actualis justitia. Sicut videre est apud Bell. de Justif. lib. 4. cap. 10. & apud Becanum in summa Theologiae Scolasticae, tom. 2. tract. 4. cap. 4. cujus titulus est, De merito bonorum operum ex sententia Calvinistarum.
latin.2698: XXVIII. Unde est quod, hac falsa nitentes hypothesi, cum inter nos & ipsos controversiae statum ponunt qui plane nullus est, hunc scilicet, Utrum homines justificati, & gratia Domini adjuvante, possint ita legem divinam implere, ut opera ipsorum, non modo non sint appellanda peccata, sed etiam vere ac proprie justa dici mereantur. Quae sunt verba Bellarmini capite illo 10. jam citato. Quibus conformia sunt quae leguntur apud Gabrielem Vasquez tom. 2. in 1. 2. disp. 212. cujus titulus est, An justi homines possint ita adimplere legem, ut ipsorum opera, non modo non sint peccata, sed etiam justa dicenda sint.
latin.2699: XXIX. Verum nunquam fuit animus Protestantium quicquam horum negare. Non docent justificatis legem Dei esse plane impossibilem. Non inficiantur fideles veram Dei mandatis praestare obedientiam, & legem Dei per Christi gratiam sic a piis impleri, ut opera bona faciant. Nec dicunt opera, quibus divino spiritu movente legi se conformare student, appellanda esse peccata, & revera talia natura sua esse: sed fatentur illa posse & debere sancta & justa dici. Id solum ab ipsis est perpetuo negatum, a fidelibus legem impleri posse perfecte, quia illorum obedientia, quamvis vera & sincera sit, longe tamen a summa perfectione semper abest.
latin.2700: XXX. Ac nequis calumnietur Protestantes diversum sentire, & nos alienam ipsis affingere doctrinam, hac de re quaedam eorum testimonia velut in specimen proferemus. Nam singula persequi infinitae operae, & superfluum esset. Et res alioqui est attendenti per se satis manifesta. Igitur Paraeus scribens in Bellar. lib. 4. de Justif. cap. 10. In quaestione, inquit, est, An justificati possint legem divinam implere, quod adversarius absolute affirmat, nos de impletione imperfecta, inchoata damus, de perfecta negamus. Et postea explicans quid sit legem implere, Legem Dei implere, inquit, si absolute loquaris, est legi divinae obedientiam perfectam, sine ullo defectu, praestare, quod justificatos non posse nos docere fateor. Quibus subjungit nos docere homini justificato legem implere impossibile esse, non plane, ut nobis falso imponit Bellarminus, sed quoad legis ἀκρίβειαν, quae omnem defectum excludit, adeoque hominem in statu gratiae posse legem implere inchoate, hoc est, novam obedientiam legis, secundum omnia ejus praecepta inchoare: non posse vero implere absolute sine omni peccato.
latin.2701: XXXI. Similia tradit Guilielmus Amesius in Bellarmino enervato tom. 4. lib. 6. c. 7. Nos, inquit, non docemus legem esse plane impossibilem homini, Adamo puta, ante lapsum, & postea Christo: necnon iis qui in Christo perfecte sanctificantur, sed de aliis, qui inchoatam tantum sanctificationem habent, ex ordinaria gratiae in ista vita dispensatione, ut legem divinam perfecte & exacte observent, nos dicimus hoc fieri non posse. Et postea, Respondens ad argumenta Bellarmini, concedit sanctos, qui in scriptura laudantur, observasse mandata proposito & conatu, non omnimodo effectu: quoad essentiam, non quoad complementum: quoad qualitatem sinceritatis, non quoad quantitatem intensionis, vel extensionis.
latin.2702: XXXII. Eodem recidunt quae habet Joannes Davenantius de justitia actuali, c. 47. Etenim excutiens canonem illum Tridentinum, Si quis dixerit Dei praecepta homini justificato, & sub gratia constituto esse ad observandum impossibilia, anathema sit. Observatis velim, inquit, in hoc Canone fabricando artem Papisticam. Norunt adversarii nostros non negare Renatis diligentem observationem praeceptorum divinorum, sed negare perfectam illam & absolutam observationem, quae legi ita cumulate satisfacit, ut nullum ejus apicem violet; quae pactum legale ita adimplet, ut ejusdem beneficio vitae aeternae haereditatem consequatur. Frustra igitur haec anathematum fulmina contra Protestantes jaculantur, qui non asserunt esse impossibile Renatis observare praecepta Dei, studiose enim in illorum omnium observatione se exercent: sed esse impossibile observando justitiam legis adaequare, & omnem ἀνομίαν effugere.
latin.2703: XXXIII. Denique Robertus Baronius Scotus, in Academia Abredonensi Theologiae Professor, tractatum brevem edidit de possibilitate implendi legem Dei consideratam secundum ἐπιείκειαν Evangelicam, quem subjunxit, instar appendicis, disputationi de peccato mortali & veniali, ubi distinguit inter obedientiam quam lex Evangelio opposita exigit, ab eo qui, vi foederis legalis, ad vitam & foelicitatem pervenire contendit, juxta solennem illam clausulam fac & vives: Et inter legis obedientiam quam ipsum Evangelium, seu foedus gratiae, ut praecise necessariam ad salutem, a nobis postulat, & sine qua neminem ad vitam aeternam admittit. Quia, licet Evangelium maximis etiam ipsis peccatoribus, & legis transgressoribus, quos lex rigide sumpta damnat, & a vita excludit, spem salutis faciat, modo serio resipiscant, & Christum fide amplectantur, neminem tamen patitur vitam aeternam sperare, qui non acta poenitentia, verum aliquod & sincerum legi divinae obsequium praestet: quandoquidem declarat sine vitae sanctimonia neminem visurum esse Dominum. Posita vero ista distinctione duplicis obedientiae, unius quam foedus operum gratiae oppositum, alterius quam ipsum foedus gratiae postulat: affirmat Doctor ille obedientiam quam foedus operum, sive lex in rigore suo considerata, ab homine exigit, homini etiam Renato non esse possibilem, neque hoc respectu legem a fidelibus ullis impleri posse: sed eam legis obedientiam quam ipsum Evangelium necessarium esse ad salutem declarat, per ordinaria gratiae auxilia regenitis esse possibilem, illosque eatenus posse legem implere, & Dei Christique mandata servare. Etenim sectione prima modo dicti tractatus haec est ejus prima assertio, Ea legis obedientia quam foedus operum, seu lex secundum rigorem suum considerata, a nobis exigit ut praecise necessariam ad salutem, neque per naturae vires, neque per ordinaria gratiae auxilia, nobis est possibilis. Secunda vero assertio sic habet, Ea legis obedientia quam Evangelium, seu foedus gratiae a nobis ut praecise necessariam ad salutem exigit, per ordinaria gratiae auxilia nobis est possibilis. Imo omnia Dei mandata, sive legalia, sive Evangelica, sigillatim ex ea parte impleri possunt, ex qua a Deo nunc proponuntur, ut stricte & praecise obligativa, sub periculo & poena damnationis aeternae.

sections.title: Even the obedience of believers has its defects
sections.pass_a: XIX. Indeed that very obedience which the faithful show to the law is not without its defects & blemishes, & in those very works which they produce in conformity with the law they do not attain the highest ἀκρίβειαν (exactness) of the law; & always in that respect there remains to them matter for progress, & something toward which they ought to strive. Which is evident from the example of Paul the Apostle. For one will not easily find anyone to whom Christ granted so great a measure of grace. And yet he himself confesses that he is not yet perfect, & that he strives perpetually toward further things. Phil. 3. Not, he says, that I have already apprehended, or am already perfect: but I follow after, if in any way I may lay hold, of that for which I also was laid hold of by Christ Jesus. Brothers, I do not reckon myself to have laid hold. But one thing I do, forgetting the things which are behind, & stretching myself out to those which are before, I press on toward the mark, toward the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
pass_b: Thesis XIX. Even the obedience believers give the law has its own defects and flaws. In the very works they do in conformity with the law they fall short of the law's full exactness (ἀκρίβεια), so that in this respect there is always room left for progress, always something still to strive toward.

Paul's example makes this plain. It would be hard to find anyone to whom Christ gave so large a measure of grace, yet Paul admits he is not yet perfect and keeps reaching for what lies further on. In Philippians 3 he writes: 'Not that I have already grasped it, or am already perfect; but I press on, if somehow I may take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me. Brothers, I do not consider that I have taken hold of it. One thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching out toward what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal, for the prize of God's upward call in Christ Jesus.'

choices.why: The Greek term for the full strictness of the law that even the best works of believers fall short of; kept in Greek in the Latin.

sections.title: Objection: Scripture calls some saints perfect
sections.pass_a: XX. But, you will say, the Apostle himself in that place supposes that some are perfect, & places himself in their number. For to the words quoted he adds, as many therefore as are perfect, let us be thus minded. And 1 Cor. 2. We speak wisdom, he says, among the perfect. And to many holy men testimony is borne in Scripture that they were perfect. So it is said of Noah Gen. 6. Noah was a just man & perfect in his generations, & walked with God. And of Job God himself, addressing Satan, says, Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, Isch Tham, that is, A man upright, or, perfect, & right, & fearing God, & turning away from evil? chap. 1. & 2. Indeed David, Psal. 18. does not fear to attribute such perfection to himself. I was, he says, unspotted, or perfect, with him, & I kept myself from my iniquity. And the Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness, & according to the cleanness of my hands in the sight of his eyes.
pass_b: Thesis XX. Someone will object that in that very passage the apostle assumes some people are perfect and counts himself among them. Right after the words just quoted he adds, 'Let as many of us as are perfect think this way.' In 1 Corinthians 2 he says, 'We speak wisdom among the perfect.'

Scripture also testifies of many holy men that they were perfect. Of Noah, Genesis 6 says: 'Noah was a righteous man and perfect in his generations, and he walked with God.' Of Job, God himself says to Satan in chapters 1 and 2: 'Have you considered my servant Job, that there is no one like him on earth, Isch Tham, that is, a man of integrity, or perfect, and upright, who fears God and turns away from evil?'

David in Psalm 18 does not even shrink from claiming such perfection: 'I was blameless, or perfect, with him, and kept myself from my iniquity. And the Lord repaid me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his sight.'

sections.title: Absolute perfection and comparative perfection
sections.pass_a: XXI. To solve which difficulty a twofold distinction of perfection must be observed. For there is a certain perfection so called absolutely, but another in a certain respect & only comparatively. Absolutely perfect is that to which nothing is lacking in its kind. But comparatively those things are called perfect which, although they are far from the highest perfection, yet surpass many others of the same kind, with which their comparison is made. When we say that in this life none are perfect, or such as render a perfect obedience to the divine will, we understand this of absolute perfection, which reaches the summit, & to which nothing can be added, in which sense Paul acknowledges that he is not yet perfect, because he had not yet reached that degree of love & obedience toward God, to which the blessed spirits reigning with Christ have been raised; whose not only knowledge, but obedience also & love, can take no further increase, since they are borne toward God with absolutely all their powers, & with the whole affection of their will. But this does not prevent the faithful who excel the rest in virtue, & who have made greater progress in the knowledge of divine truth, & in the pursuit of piety & righteousness, from being named perfect, not indeed simply, but in respect of those who yield much to them in this part, & who are still, as Paul speaks, infants in Christ, & in a manner carnal, in comparison with those who in a singular way are called spiritual, as is to be seen 1 Cor. 3. And these are among Christians, so to speak, the more grown up, & of a more advanced age & stature, if one may speak so, whom Paul in the places cited before calls perfect, when he says, We speak wisdom among the perfect, &, As many as are perfect, let us be thus minded.
pass_b: Thesis XXI. To resolve this difficulty we need a twofold distinction of perfection. One kind is called perfection absolutely; the other is perfection only in a certain respect, by comparison. What is absolutely perfect lacks nothing in its kind. Things are called perfect by comparison when, though far short of the highest perfection, they still surpass many other things of the same kind with which they are compared.

When we say that no one in this life is perfect, that is, no one gives God's will a perfect obedience, we mean absolute perfection: perfection that has reached the top and can receive no addition. In this sense Paul admits he is not yet perfect, since he had not yet reached the degree of love and obedience toward God to which the blessed spirits reigning with Christ have been raised. Their knowledge, and their obedience and love as well, can grow no further, because they are carried toward God with all their powers and the whole affection of their will.

None of this stops believers who outstrip others in virtue, and who have advanced further in knowing divine truth and in striving after piety and righteousness, from being called perfect. They are perfect not simply, but relative to those who fall well behind them here: those who are still, in Paul's words, infants in Christ and in some way carnal, compared with others who are called spiritual in a special sense (see 1 Corinthians 3). These are, so to speak, the grown-ups among Christians, of a riper age and stature, if one may put it so. They are the ones Paul calls perfect in the passages cited, when he says, 'We speak wisdom among the perfect,' and, 'Let as many of us as are perfect think this way.'

choices.why: Perfection that reaches the highest point and admits no addition, as against perfection only 'in a certain respect and by comparison'.

sections.title: Perfection of parts and perfection of degrees
sections.pass_a: XXII. Akin to this distinction is another, according to which perfection is usually divided into perfection of parts & perfection of degrees. Obedience perfect according to degrees is that which attains the highest degree of perfection, & through which someone so perfectly conforms & submits himself to the law, that nothing at all can be found wanting in him, nor in this respect can he make progress for the better. In this way we contend, & it is manifest of itself, that the law is fulfilled perfectly by no one in this life. But obedience which is far from the highest degree of perfection, can nevertheless be & be called perfect according to its parts; since in respect of the parts, whether essential, or integral, nothing is lacking to it of those things which are necessary that it may be true obedience & acceptable to God. In this sense the obedience of the godly in this life is perfect, & in this respect the faithful who are renewed by the grace of Christ, & are led by his spirit, can perfectly fulfil the law of God, that is, render to his commandments a true & sincere, & to God pleasing obedience. For the essential perfection of such a thing is nothing other than the truth & sincerity of the thing itself.
pass_b: Thesis XXII. Close to this distinction is another, which commonly divides perfection into perfection of parts and perfection of degrees. Obedience perfect in degree reaches the highest degree of perfection: through it a person conforms and submits himself to the law so perfectly that nothing at all can be found lacking in him and he can make no further improvement in that respect. In this sense, as we maintain and as is self-evident, no one fulfils the law perfectly in this life.

Obedience that falls well short of the highest degree can still be, and be called, perfect in its parts. As to its parts, essential or integral, it lacks none of what is needed for true obedience acceptable to God. In this sense the obedience of the godly in this life is perfect, and in this respect believers renewed by Christ's grace and led by his Spirit can fulfil God's law perfectly: that is, they can give his commandments a true, sincere obedience that pleases God. The essential perfection of such a thing is simply its being true and sincere.

lemmas.gloss: perfection of parts and perfection of degrees
whether essential, or integral
the truth and sincerity of the thing itself

choices.why: The scholastic distinction: nothing essential missing (parts) versus the highest degree reached (degrees).
rejected: perfection of portions and of grades

sections.title: Three requirements of true obedience
sections.pass_a: XXIII. But that this may become clearer, it must be observed that for this, that our obedience be true & sincere, three things chiefly are required. The first is that it be rendered not only with the body & outward work, but also with the inward affection of the mind. For it profits nothing to do those things which the law commands, unless it be done out of love for God, & out of zeal for fulfilling his will & promoting his glory. As neither is it enough to have a certain affection of obeying God, unless his commandments, when the matter requires it, are carried out in the work itself. Moreover it does not suffice for true obedience that we keep certain commandments of God, the rest neglected: but it is necessary that we seriously submit ourselves to all the precepts of the Divine law, & strive to fulfil them, when occasion offers itself. Lastly our obedience ought to be constant & persevering: Nor is it enough to obey God for a time, but in his obedience, through adverse things as well as through prosperous things, one must persevere right to the end.
pass_b: Thesis XXIII. To make this clearer, note that three things above all are needed for our obedience to be true and sincere. First, it must be given not only with the body and outward action but with the inner affection of the mind as well. Doing what the law commands profits nothing unless it springs from love of God and from zeal to carry out his will and advance his glory. Equally, a certain wish to obey God is not enough unless his commandments are actually carried out in deed when the situation calls for it.

Second, true obedience is not satisfied by keeping some of God's commandments while neglecting the rest. We must earnestly submit to every precept of the divine law and try to fulfil each one as occasions arise. Third, our obedience must be steady and lasting. Obeying God for a while is not enough; we have to persevere in obeying him to the end, in hard times as in good ones.

sections.title: The regenerate lack none of these
sections.pass_a: XXIV. In respect of all these nothing is lacking to the obedience of those who are truly godly & reborn by the spirit of God. For they do not serve God with the body only, but subject the mind & affections to his will. Nor do they only perform in work what is commanded in the law; but also in it they look to the glory of God, & are moved by love for him. They do not take care to obey merely these, or those commandments; but strive to conform themselves to the whole law of God & to each of its commandments. Nor only for some time, & so long as things flow prosperously, but also when temptations & persecutions rush upon them, & right up to the last breath of life they have the commandments of God before their eyes, & regulate their actions to their rule.
pass_b: Thesis XXIV. On all these counts, the obedience of the truly godly, those reborn by God's Spirit, lacks nothing. They serve God not with the body alone but bring mind and affections under his will. They not only do in deed what the law commands; in doing it they aim at God's glory and are moved by love for him.

Their concern is not to obey merely this or that commandment; they try to conform themselves to God's whole law and to every one of its commandments. And they do so not merely for a while, as long as things go well, but also when temptations and persecutions break upon them: to their last breath they keep God's commandments before their eyes and measure their actions by that rule.

sections.title: This is the perfection of parts Scripture praises
sections.pass_a: XXV. Therefore by full right that perfection can be attributed to their obedience, which is usually called the perfection of Parts in the Schools. Since they try to conform to the whole law, & to all its precepts, both the acts of the body, & the affections of the mind, & that constantly & perseveringly. And certainly, were this not so, Scripture would not attribute to the faithful true righteousness & holiness, when it says that they put on the new man, who is created according to God, in righteousness & holiness of truth, Ephes. 4. For it is not true righteousness, which in respect of the parts, that belong wholly to the essence of righteousness, is maimed & mutilated. And this is that perfection in the name of which Job & Noah are praised, & which David does not dread to attribute to himself. For by perfection there is designated only the integrity & sincerity of those holy men. Since the Hebrew word Tham or thamim, which the Interpreters there render by perfect, properly means upright & sincere.
pass_b: Thesis XXV. So the perfection the Schools usually call perfection of parts can rightly be ascribed to their obedience. They try to bring both the acts of the body and the affections of the mind into line with the whole law and every one of its precepts, and to do so steadily and with perseverance.

If this were not so, Scripture would certainly not credit believers with true righteousness and holiness, as it does in Ephesians 4 when it says they put on the new man, created after God in the righteousness and holiness of truth. A righteousness maimed and mutilated in the parts that belong to its very essence is no true righteousness.

This is the perfection for which Job and Noah are praised and which David has no qualms about claiming for himself. In those places 'perfection' means only the integrity and sincerity of these holy men; the Hebrew word Tham or thamim, which translators there render 'perfect', properly means whole and sincere.

sections.title: The orthodox position stated
sections.pass_a: XXVI. We deny therefore that the faithful can perfectly fulfil the law of God, if the talk is of the perfection which is called absolute & of degrees: both because all of them, no less than other men, are sinners by nature; & because after receiving grace they do not cease to offend in many things, & remain liable even to grave falls: nor in the very good works which they do do they attain that highest ἀκρίβειαν (exactness), which the law in its rigour demands. And yet with Scripture we say & teach, that the faithful keep the commandments of God through the grace of Christ, & in some manner also fulfil the law, since they show to the divine law a true & God-approved obedience, according to all its precepts: which obedience, although it sinks far below the highest perfection, nevertheless, according to the style of Scripture, can be called perfect; since it is true & sincere, nor is anything lacking to it of those things which are necessarily required for the nature & integrity of a true obedience acceptable to God.
pass_b: Thesis XXVI. So we deny that believers can fulfil God's law perfectly, if the perfection meant is the one called absolute, the perfection of degrees. All of them, no less than other people, are sinners by nature; even after receiving grace they keep stumbling in many things and stay exposed to serious falls; and in their good works themselves they fall short of the full exactness (ἀκρίβεια) the law demands in its strictness.

Yet with Scripture we say and teach that believers keep God's commandments by Christ's grace, and in a certain way fulfil the law as well, since they give the divine law a true obedience, approved by God, that covers all its precepts. That obedience sits far below the highest perfection, but in Scripture's usage it can still be called perfect, because it is true and sincere and lacks nothing that the nature and integrity of true obedience, acceptable to God, necessarily requires.

sections.title: Roman doctors misstate the Reformed doctrine
sections.pass_a: XXVII. And this explanation of the Orthodox Opinion must be carefully observed on account of the doctors of the Roman Church, who in this question, as in many others, either do not understand the doctrine of the Reformed School, or pervert it on purpose. Since they attribute to the Protestant Theologians that they simply deny that the faithful of Christ can keep the commandments of God, & so fulfil the law, that some of their works can be called just. Indeed that they teach that the law is plainly impossible to a man even justified through the grace of Christ: so that he cannot do any good works, nor is there in him any true actual righteousness. As can be seen in Bell. de Justif. book 4. chap. 10. & in Becanus in the summa of Scholastic Theology, tom. 2. tract. 4. chap. 4. whose title is, On the merit of good works according to the opinion of the Calvinists.
pass_b: Thesis XXVII. This account of the orthodox view needs careful attention because of the doctors of the Roman Church, who on this question, as on many others, either fail to understand the teaching of the Reformed school or twist it deliberately. They ascribe to Protestant theologians a flat denial that Christ's faithful can keep God's commandments and fulfil the law in such a way that any of their works can be called righteous.

They even claim that Protestants teach that the law is simply impossible for someone justified by Christ's grace, so that he can do no good works at all and has no true actual righteousness. This can be seen in Bellarmine, De justificatione, book 4, chapter 10, and in Becanus's Summa of scholastic theology, volume 2, tractate 4, chapter 4, which is titled 'On the merit of good works according to the opinion of the Calvinists'.

sections.title: A state of the question that does not exist
sections.pass_a: XXVIII. Whence it is that, leaning on this false hypothesis, they set up between us & themselves a state of the controversy which is plainly none at all, namely this, Whether justified men, & with the grace of the Lord helping, can so fulfil the divine law, that their works, not only are not to be called sins, but also deserve to be called truly & properly just. Which are the words of Bellarmine in that chapter 10 already cited. With which agree those things which are read in Gabriel Vasquez tom. 2. on 1. 2. disp. 212. whose title is, Whether just men can so fulfil the law, that their works, not only are not sins, but also are to be called just.
pass_b: Thesis XXVIII. Hence, resting on this false assumption, they frame between us and them a state of the controversy that does not exist at all, namely 'whether justified people, helped by the Lord's grace, can fulfil the divine law in such a way that their works not only should not be called sins but truly and properly deserve to be called righteous.' These are Bellarmine's words in the chapter 10 already cited.

In line with them is what we read in Gabriel Vasquez, volume 2 on the Prima Secundae, disputation 212, whose title asks 'whether righteous people can fulfil the law in such a way that their works are not only not sins but are to be called righteous.'

sections.title: What Protestants do and do not deny
sections.pass_a: XXIX. But it was never the mind of the Protestants to deny any of these things. They do not teach that the law of God is plainly impossible to the justified. They do not deny that the faithful render true obedience to the commandments of God, & that the law of God is so fulfilled by the godly through the grace of Christ, that they do good works. Nor do they say that the works, by which, the divine spirit moving them, they study to conform themselves to the law, are to be called sins, & are really such by their nature: but they confess that they can & ought to be called holy & just. This alone has perpetually been denied by them, that the law can be fulfilled perfectly by the faithful, because their obedience, although it be true & sincere, is yet always far from the highest perfection.
pass_b: Thesis XXIX. Protestants never meant to deny any of this. They do not teach that God's law is simply impossible for the justified. They do not deny that believers give God's commandments true obedience, or that by Christ's grace the godly fulfil God's law to the extent of doing good works.

Nor do they say that the works by which believers, moved by the divine Spirit, try to conform themselves to the law must be called sins and are really sins by nature; they grant that such works can and should be called holy and righteous. The one thing they have always denied is that believers can fulfil the law perfectly, since their obedience, however true and sincere, always falls far short of the highest perfection.

sections.title: The testimony of Pareus
sections.pass_a: XXX. And lest anyone slander that the Protestants think differently, & that we foist on them a doctrine foreign to them, we will bring forward some of their testimonies on this matter as a specimen. For to pursue them one by one would be a work of infinite labour, & superfluous. And the matter is otherwise manifest enough of itself to one who pays attention. Accordingly Pareus writing on Bellar. book 4. de Justif. chap. 10. In question, he says, is, Whether the justified can fulfil the divine law, which the adversary affirms absolutely, we grant concerning an imperfect, begun fulfilment, we deny concerning the perfect. And afterwards explaining what it is to fulfil the law, To fulfil the law of God, he says, if you speak absolutely, is to render to the divine law a perfect obedience, without any defect, which I confess we teach the justified cannot do. To which he adds that we teach that to fulfil the law is impossible for the justified man, not plainly, as Bellarmine falsely imputes to us, but as to the ἀκρίβειαν (exactness) of the law, which excludes every defect, & accordingly that man in the state of grace can fulfil the law inchoately, that is, begin the new obedience of the law, according to all its precepts: but cannot fulfil it absolutely without any sin.
pass_b: Thesis XXX. So that no one can falsely allege that Protestants think otherwise, or that we are pinning on them a doctrine not their own, we will cite a few of their statements on the matter as a sample. To go through them all would be endless labour, and needless; besides, the matter is plain enough to anyone who pays attention.

Pareus, then, writing on Bellarmine's De justificatione, book 4, chapter 10, says: 'The question is whether the justified can fulfil the divine law. Our opponent affirms it absolutely; we grant it of an imperfect, begun fulfilment and deny it of a perfect one.' Later, explaining what fulfilling the law means, he says: 'To fulfil God's law, speaking absolutely, is to give the divine law a perfect obedience without any defect, and I confess we teach that the justified cannot do this.'

He goes on to say that we teach fulfilling the law is impossible for a justified person, not outright, as Bellarmine falsely charges us, but with respect to the law's exactness (ἀκρίβεια), which rules out every defect. A person in the state of grace can therefore fulfil the law in a begun way, that is, begin the new obedience of the law according to all its precepts, but cannot fulfil it absolutely, without any sin.

sections.title: The testimony of Ames
sections.pass_a: XXXI. Ames teaches similar things in Bellarminus enervatus tom. 4. book 6. ch. 7. We, he says, do not teach that the law is plainly impossible for man, for Adam, say, before the fall, & afterwards for Christ: nor for those who are perfectly sanctified in Christ, but concerning others, who have only a begun sanctification, according to the ordinary dispensation of grace in this life, that they should observe the divine law perfectly & exactly, we say that this cannot be done. And afterwards, Answering the arguments of Bellarmine, he grants that the saints, who are praised in Scripture, observed the commandments in purpose & endeavour, not in every way in effect: as to essence, not as to completion: as to the quality of sincerity, not as to the quantity of intension, or extension.
pass_b: Thesis XXXI. William Ames says much the same in Bellarminus enervatus, volume 4, book 6, chapter 7: 'We do not teach that the law is simply impossible for man: for Adam, say, before the fall, and afterwards for Christ, or for those perfectly sanctified in Christ. But of others, whose sanctification is only begun under the ordinary dispensation of grace in this life, we say that they cannot keep the divine law perfectly and exactly.'

Later, replying to Bellarmine's arguments, he grants that the saints praised in Scripture kept the commandments in purpose and effort, though not completely in effect; in essence, not in completion; in the quality of sincerity, not in the quantity of intensity or extent.

sections.title: The testimony of Davenant on the Tridentine canon
sections.pass_a: XXXII. To the same come the things which John Davenant has on actual righteousness, ch. 47. For examining that Tridentine canon, If anyone says that the precepts of God are impossible to observe for a man justified, & set under grace, let him be anathema. Observe, I pray, he says, in framing this Canon the Papist art. The adversaries know that ours do not deny to the Regenerate a diligent observance of the divine precepts, but deny that perfect & absolute observance, which so abundantly satisfies the law, that it violates not a jot of it; which so fulfils the legal covenant, that by its benefit it obtains the inheritance of eternal life. In vain therefore do they hurl these thunderbolts of anathemas against the Protestants, who do not assert that it is impossible for the Regenerate to observe the precepts of God, for they exercise themselves diligently in the observance of them all: but that it is impossible by observing to equal the righteousness of the law, & to escape all ἀνομίαν (lawlessness).
pass_b: Thesis XXXII. John Davenant's remarks on actual righteousness, chapter 47, come to the same thing. Examining the Tridentine canon 'If anyone says that God's precepts are impossible to keep for a man who is justified and placed under grace, let him be anathema,' he writes: 'Notice, please, the papist craft in framing this canon.

Our opponents know that our side does not deny the regenerate a diligent keeping of the divine precepts. What we deny is the perfect and absolute keeping that satisfies the law so fully that it breaks not one jot of it, and fulfils the legal covenant so completely that by virtue of it one gains the inheritance of eternal life.

So they hurl these thunderbolts of anathema at the Protestants in vain. Protestants do not claim that the regenerate cannot keep God's precepts, for they work hard at keeping all of them. They claim that it is impossible, by keeping them, to match the law's righteousness and escape all lawlessness (ἀνομία).'

sections.title: The testimony of Robert Baron
sections.pass_a: XXXIII. Lastly Robert Baron, a Scot, Professor of Theology in the Academy of Aberdeen, published a brief treatise on the possibility of fulfilling the law of God considered according to Evangelical ἐπιείκειαν (equity), which he added, as an appendix, to the disputation on mortal & venial sin, where he distinguishes between the obedience which the law opposed to the Gospel demands, from him who, by force of the legal covenant, strives to come to life & happiness, according to that solemn clause do & you will live: And the obedience of the law which the Gospel itself, or the covenant of grace, requires of us as precisely necessary to salvation, & without which it admits no one to eternal life. Because, although the Gospel gives hope of salvation even to the very greatest sinners, & transgressors of the law, whom the law taken rigidly condemns, & excludes from life, provided they seriously repent, & embrace Christ by faith, yet it suffers no one to hope for eternal life, who does not, having done repentance, render some true & sincere obedience to the divine law: since it declares that without holiness of life no one will see the Lord. But this distinction of a twofold obedience being laid down, one which the covenant of works opposed to grace, the other which the covenant of grace itself requires: that Doctor affirms that the obedience which the covenant of works, or the law considered in its rigour, demands from man, is not possible even for the Regenerate man, nor in this respect can the law be fulfilled by any of the faithful: but that the obedience of the law which the Gospel itself declares to be necessary to salvation, is possible for the regenerate through the ordinary helps of grace, & that they so far can fulfil the law, & keep the commandments of God & of Christ. For in the first section of the said treatise this is his first assertion, That obedience of the law which the covenant of works, or the law considered according to its rigour, demands of us as precisely necessary to salvation, is possible for us neither through the powers of nature, nor through the ordinary helps of grace. But the second assertion runs thus, That obedience of the law which the Gospel, or the covenant of grace demands of us as precisely necessary to salvation, is possible for us through the ordinary helps of grace. Indeed all the commandments of God, whether legal, or Evangelical, can be fulfilled one by one on that side, on which they are now proposed by God, as strictly & precisely binding, under peril & penalty of eternal damnation.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIII. Finally Robert Baron, a Scot and professor of theology at the Academy of Aberdeen, published a short treatise on the possibility of fulfilling God's law considered according to evangelical equity (ἐπιείκεια), which he attached as an appendix to his disputation on mortal and venial sin. There he distinguishes two kinds of obedience.

The first is the obedience demanded by the law as opposed to the Gospel, from anyone who tries to reach life and happiness by virtue of the legal covenant, under its solemn clause 'Do and you will live'. The second is the obedience to the law that the Gospel itself, the covenant of grace, requires of us as strictly necessary for salvation, without which it admits no one to eternal life.

For although the Gospel offers hope of salvation even to the greatest sinners and lawbreakers, whom the law strictly taken condemns and shuts out of life, on condition that they truly repent and embrace Christ by faith, it allows no one to hope for eternal life who does not, after repenting, give the divine law some true and sincere obedience. It declares that without holiness of life no one will see the Lord.

With this distinction between the two obediences in place, one required by the covenant of works opposed to grace and the other by the covenant of grace itself, the doctor maintains the following. The obedience that the covenant of works, the law in its strictness, demands of man is not possible even for the regenerate, and in that respect no believer can fulfil the law. But the obedience to the law that the Gospel itself declares necessary for salvation is possible for the regenerate through the ordinary helps of grace, and to that extent they can fulfil the law and keep the commandments of God and of Christ.

Indeed, in the first section of that treatise his first assertion reads: 'The obedience to the law that the covenant of works, or the law considered in its strictness, demands of us as strictly necessary for salvation is possible for us neither by the powers of nature nor by the ordinary helps of grace.' His second assertion reads: 'The obedience to the law that the Gospel, or covenant of grace, demands of us as strictly necessary for salvation is possible for us through the ordinary helps of grace. Indeed all God's commandments, legal or evangelical, can be fulfilled one by one in the respect in which God now sets them before us as strictly and precisely binding, under threat and penalty of eternal damnation.'
